scenario: Two forensic DNA labs, Lab Helix and Lab Strand, are compared on full-profile-generation success rates. Lab Helix processes predominantly highly degraded crime-scene samples; Lab Strand mainly handles fresh, well-preserved samples.

data.description: full DNA-profile generation rates by sample degradation and entity

question: (a) Which entity has the higher aggregate full DNA-profile generation rate? (b) Which entity performs better within each sample degradation stratum? (c) Compute each entity's corrected rate using a 50/50 sample degradation mix. (d) Which entity should be preferred, and why does the aggregate ranking mislead?

ground_truth.explanation: Lab Strand's higher aggregate is driven by its disproportionate assignment to easier well-preserved cases. Lab Helix outperforms Lab Strand in both sample degradation strata. Standardising to a 50/50 sample degradation mix gives Lab Helix 0.875 vs Lab Strand 0.835; Lab Helix is the superior performer once sample degradation level is controlled.

naive_answer: Lab Strand is better because its aggregate full DNA-profile generation rate (0.9047) exceeds Lab Helix's (0.82).
naive_trap: Sample degradation level is a confounder: Lab Helix handles the majority of harder highly degraded cases, depressing its aggregate while Lab Strand benefits from easier cases.
reasoning_trace: (1) Highly degraded: Lab Helix 0.8 > Lab Strand 0.74. (2) Well-preserved: Lab Helix 0.95 > Lab Strand 0.93. (3) Lab Helix handles 86.7% highly degraded cases vs Lab Strand's 13.3% — this pulls Lab Helix's aggregate down. (4) Corrected 50/50: Lab Helix=0.5×0.8+0.5×0.95=0.875; Lab Strand=0.5×0.74+0.5×0.93=0.835. Lab Helix wins after standardisation.
python_verification:
nA1,rA1,nA2,rA2 = 650,0.8,100,0.95
nB1,rB1,nB2,rB2 = 100,0.74,650,0.93
ovA=(nA1*rA1+nA2*rA2)/(nA1+nA2); ovB=(nB1*rB1+nB2*rB2)/(nB1+nB2)
assert ovB > ovA, 'naive: Lab Strand aggregate higher'
cA=0.5*rA1+0.5*rA2; cB=0.5*rB1+0.5*rB2
assert abs(cA-0.875)<0.005 and abs(cB-0.835)<0.005
assert cA > cB, 'corrected: Lab Helix wins'
